paras: The attempted lynching of Lee Lung took place in Union Hill, New Jersey, on or about January 12, 1888, when a crowd gathered at the laundry of Lee Lung, a Chinese man, and prepared to lynch him after a seventeen-year-old girl accused him of attempting to assault her. A policeman sent to arrest him persuaded the crowd to desist, took him out by a rear door and brought him before the local recorder, who released him on $500 bail. Two New York papers reported the case the next morning, and a press dispatch carried it to the Pacific coast under the headline "A Mongolian Brute."

Lee Lung kept a laundry on Bergen Line Avenue in Union Hill, where, according to The Sun, he had been washing linen for several months. Lydia Giboran, aged seventeen, went to the laundry to collect clothes she had left to be washed and found him alone.

The accounts, which gave only the girl's version, stated that Lee attempted to assault her; The Sun said he forced her to the floor and that she fought and screamed. Drawn by her cries, a young man named Mullins broke in, pulled her away and, in the Tribune's words, gave Lee "a sound thrashing." The girl then told her story at Recorder Schleicher's court, and the recorder sent Policeman Stahl to arrest Lee.

Meanwhile the story spread among the neighbors and an angry crowd gathered in front of the laundry. According to the Tribune, preparations were being made to take Lee out and lynch him, and the wire dispatch said the crowd was "preparing to hang him." The Sun reported that the crowd was muttering threats, that the policeman forced his way through it with difficulty, and that he warned it not to follow him or molest his prisoner. Inside, Lee was found shaking with fright in a dark corner of the kitchen and begged for protection, The Sun said. Stahl persuaded the crowd to desist and took his prisoner out by the rear door, a move The Sun described as cleverly deceiving the crowd, and brought him before the recorder.

The recorder held Lee under $500 bonds, which the Tribune said were furnished by his landlord and The Sun identified as Mr. Palmer, owner of the building Lee occupied. Once released, Lee left at once; the Tribune said he did not dare return to his shop, and The Sun said he immediately shook the dust of Union Hill from his feet. No report of a later hearing or trial on the charge, or of any action against members of the crowd, appears in the coverage.

The New-York Tribune ran the story on January 13 under the headline "Preparing to Lynch a Chinaman," with the subhead "A Union Hill, N. J., Mob Exasperated by an Attempt at Assault," and called Lee "the scoundrel." The Sun, the same morning, called him a "Celestial" and opened in a jocular tone, saying he had come "precious near dangling at the end of a rope," while crediting the policeman's handling of the crowd. Neither New York paper questioned the girl's accusation or reported anything Lee said in his own defense.

A California Associated Press dispatch dated New York, January 13, appeared in the Sacramento Daily Record-Union on January 14 under the headlines "A Mongolian Brute" and "Attempt of a Chinaman to Outrage a Young White Girl," the only account to state the girl's race. The same dispatch ran on January 20 in a column of clipped dispatches in the State Rights Democrat of Albany, Oregon, which printed the girl's name as "Lydia Gibson" and placed the incident "yesterday."

The accounts differ on the date: the Tribune and The Sun, both published January 13, placed the incident "yesterday," January 12, while the Sacramento printing of the dispatch dated January 13 said "today." Because the two New York reports were written independently and agree, January 12 is the better-supported date. The Sun first printed the name as "Leo Yung" and thereafter called him "Lee," while the other accounts give "Lee Lung" throughout.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Lee Lung
bases: A crowd gathered at a Chinese laundryman's shop and prepared to lynch or hang him after a girl accused him of attempted assault, until a policeman removed him (A1, A2, A3).

No one was killed: the crowd prepared to lynch Lee Lung over an accusation of attempted assault but a policeman took him away and he was released on bail (A1, A2, A3), so this was a threatened lynching, not a completed one.

The Tribune and The Sun gave independent accounts with different details that agree on the accusation, the crowd preparing to lynch him and the policeman's removal of him, and a wire dispatch repeats the core story (A1, A2, A3).

accounts.label: New-York Tribune
accounts.gist: Lee attempted to assault the girl, Mullins thrashed him, and an angry crowd was preparing to lynch him when Policeman Stahl persuaded it to desist and took him to the recorder.

accounts.label: The Sun (New York)
accounts.gist: Lee forced the girl to the floor; a crowd muttering threats collected, the policeman forced his way in, found Lee shaking with fright and slipped him out the rear door.

accounts.label: Wire report (California Associated Press)
accounts.gist: Lee narrowly escaped lynching; police had hard work getting him away from a crowd preparing to hang him.

framing.detail: The Tribune headlined 'Preparing to Lynch a Chinaman' and 'Mob Exasperated by an Attempt at Assault', called Lee 'the scoundrel', and presented the accusation as fact while crediting the policeman with stopping the crowd.
The Sun treated the case lightly ('came precious near dangling at the end of a rope'), called him a 'Celestial', and praised the policeman for 'cleverly' deceiving the crowd.
The wire dispatch ran under 'A Mongolian Brute' and 'Attempt of a Chinaman to Outrage a Young White Girl'.

conflicts.note: Two independent New York morning papers agree on Jan. 12; the Oregon printing of the same dispatch (A4) also reads 'yesterday', so 'today' in A3 is likely an editing change.
One person; The Sun's first-mention variant is the source of the 'Leo' form.
